pages.name: Closing, the morning, and the phone

artboards.title: Proposed — the morning, un-gated, and the two other banners

annotations.text:
WHAT I TOOK FROM YOUR ANSWERS, AND FROM YOUR REVIEW

Second pass. Your review was right about three things and this build backs them out.

THE DAY'S MOVEMENTS IS THE TABLE AS IT WAS — same columns (Time, Account, Type, Category with its description, In, Out, That account now), same rhythm, same footer totals, same account filter. I had replaced Type with a source line and narrowed the description; that was a loss, not a gain. The one thing that changed is the row's actions: two marks instead of the words Edit and Delete printed eighteen times down a nine-row table.

THE DONUTS ARE BACK, in the house palette rather than ten colours the app does not own. One hue per side — verdigris for money in, crimson for money out — dark to light in size order, so the ring and the list read the same way round and green still means in the way it does everywhere else in the app. A transfer is neither earned nor spent, so it is steel in both rings and the note under each says what that grey slice is. The total moved into the middle of the ring, where the old separate total row was, and the two round + / − buttons are gone because Log a movement is now permanently on screen above.

WHAT SURVIVES FROM THE FIRST PASS, as you asked: Money on hand as a five-figure strip, Log a movement as a line that stays open, and the whole right rail — closing state and the count, what needs your eye, and the last seven days.

THE DAY IS STILL THE UNIT and the opening gate is still gone; those were your first two answers and nothing here changes them.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Creditors and Purchase invoices.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. THE WHOLE BOOK IS BEHIND A GATE. Until three opening figures are confirmed, the cash book is REPLACED by a form. You cannot see yesterday, you cannot see today's movements, you cannot log a seven-in-the-morning sale. And on every morning but the first, all three figures are already known — the app carried them itself. It is a form asking you to confirm what it just worked out, standing in front of everything.

2. THE ACCENT IS SPENT ON A FIGURE. Money on hand sits on an oxide-soft ground in oxide-deep ink. The palette's own rule is that a figure is a size, not a warning, and that the accent appears once, on the one thing to do next. Here it marks a number you cannot act on, so nothing on the screen says what to do — and Money in wears the same accent, so there are two.

3. FIVE BUTTONS OF EQUAL WEIGHT in the day header — Money in, Money out, Transfer, Opening, Print. Two of them are the job. "Opening" edits the figures the whole book is measured from and sits between Transfer and Print like a peer.

4. EVERY ENTRY IS A MODAL. Logging a sale and three expenses is four dialogs opened and dismissed. Each one hides the ledger you are adding to, so you cannot see the entry land.

5. NOTHING IS CHECKED. A day left uncounted behind you, a count that came up short and was never booked, an account that has not moved in a fortnight — none of it is surfaced. The chain-break warning exists, but it only fires when the opening figure disagrees with the day before, which is one fault out of several the data can already answer.

6. NO HISTORY WITHOUT WALKING. Reading last Tuesday means pressing ‹ six times, and there is no sign on the way which of those days was ever counted.

7. THE COUNT SITS HALF-DONE AT THE FOOT OF THE PAGE, below the fold, all day. Three cards with three empty boxes are the last thing on a screen whose most important act they are.

8. THE DONUTS ARE THE RIGHT SHAPE IN THE WRONG COLOURS — ten of them, #2F7D4F, #F2A93C, #3B82C4, #8E5FD1 and six more, none of the 23. The green in them is not the app's verdigris and the red is not its crimson, so "good" and "bad" mean something different in this one panel. And a transfer is drawn as an ordinary slice in both rings, so the day's in and out each carry half a million the shop neither earned nor spent, with nothing on screen saying so.

9. TWO ROUND FLOATING BUTTONS, + and −, sitting on top of the charts, duplicating Money in and Money out from the top of the page — with a drop shadow, where depth in this app is hairlines.

10. A 190-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH ABOVE THE WORK, unmeasured, describing what a cash book is to somebody who has opened it every morning for a year.

11. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES: 10.5 / 11.5 / 12.5 / 13.5 type, radius 10 and 12, weight 700 where the ramp says 600, and a card shadow.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

WHAT READS FIRST IS MONEY ON HAND, in ink, at 27px, with what the day opened at underneath it. It is the question the screen is opened for. It is not the accent, because it is not something you do. Each account then carries its net move on the day in one figure rather than a gross pair — the gross pair is in the donuts and in the table's footer, and printing it three times was noise.

THE ACCENT IS ADD. One oxide element on the screen: the button that commits the movement you are typing. During the day that is the one thing to do next. When you go to close, it moves to Close the day and nothing else is oxide there either.

THE ENTRY LINE IS TWO ROWS AND STAYS OPEN. In / Out / Transfer as a segment — three verbs, not two plus a flavour — then amount, account, category and time; the note, which is the field that needs the width, and Add on the second row. Four expenses is four presses instead of four dialogs, and each lands in the table directly beneath where it can be seen to have landed. Transfer is a first-class verb because moving 500,000 from the bank to the drawer is neither income nor expense and filing it as either is a lie in the profit and loss.

THE DAY'S MOVEMENTS IS UNCHANGED FROM WHAT SHIPS, except for its actions. The running balance is per account and the column is still named "That account now", so nobody reads it as one total. Edit and Delete are now two 26px marks at the end of the row, dimmed until the row is under the pointer and the delete turning crimson there — eighteen labels for two acts nobody is looking for until they are.

THE DONUTS KEEP THEIR SHAPE AND LOSE THEIR PALETTE. #2F7D4F, #3B82C4, #8E5FD1 and seven more belonged to nothing; a green that is not the app's verdigris and a red that is not its crimson mean that "good" and "bad" say something different inside that one panel. Now: verdigris for in, crimson for out, darkest slice biggest, and the transfer in steel on both sides because it is the shop's own money crossing the yard. The figure sits in the hole of the ring, so the total and its parts are one object rather than a number floating above a chart.

WHAT NEEDS YOUR EYE — three checks, all derivable from what is already on file, run every time the screen draws: a count that came up short and was never booked; a day left uncounted behind you; an account that has not moved in a suspicious while. Each is one line, the evidence, the money, and one act. Crimson for the shop being out of pocket, amber for something to look at. And the note says what is NOT checked, because a checking panel whose silence you cannot read is worse than none.

THE LAST SEVEN DAYS replaces pressing the back arrow. Date, closing figure, and one dot: counted and agreed, part counted, did not match, not counted. A missing Sunday is explained rather than left as a gap.

HEIGHT: the first screen at 1440 × 900 now reaches the fifth movement, and the count — the act this screen exists for — is a rail line in the top right rather than three empty boxes below the fold.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE DONUT COLOURS ARE ONE HUE PER SIDE, dark to light in size order. It keeps green meaning in and red meaning out, and it survives a grayscale print — but two adjacent small slices are harder to tell apart than two different hues were. If the shop regularly reads six or seven categories off one ring, that ordering breaks down and the honest answer is fewer, bigger categories rather than more colours.

2. THE TRANSFER IS DRAWN AS TWO LEDGER ROWS — out of the bank, into the cash — at the same minute, which is how it ships today and what keeps each account's running balance honest. It does mean one act makes two lines and 500,000 in both donuts. I have marked it grey and said so under each ring rather than quietly removing it; the alternative is excluding transfers from the rings entirely, which is cleaner but then the ring no longer adds up to the table's footer.

3. EDIT AND DELETE ARE ICONS WITH A TITLE ONLY. On a touch screen there is no hover to reveal them, so on the phone the card opens instead — that is why the phone cards carry no buttons at all.

4. THE THIRD CHECK — "nothing through the bank in 9 days" — is the softest of the three. A shop that genuinely uses the bank twice a month will see it cry wolf. It may want a threshold you set once, or a dismissal that sticks for that account.

5. I HAVE NOT PUT A WEEK OR MONTH TOTAL ANYWHERE. You chose the day as the unit and I have kept to it. The seven-day spine shows closing balances but does not add them up.

6. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the print sheet, the transfer's effect on the profit and loss, the category presets, and the thirty-second refresh. The edit-an-entry modal survives as it is.

COUNTING THE TILL →

THIS IS THE ACT THE RAIL BECOMES. It is one region, not three cards on a page — the ledger is out of the way, because counting is a thing you do standing at the drawer with the screen in front of you, not while reading the day.

EACH ROW IS THE SENTENCE SOMEBODY ACTUALLY SAYS: this account, this is what the book expects and how it got there, this is what I counted, this is the difference and here is what a difference of that sign usually MEANS. Money short and money spare are not the same problem — short is usually a payment out that was never logged, spare is usually a sale that was never rung up — and saying so is the difference between a figure and a prompt.

NOT COUNTED IS NOT ZERO. An empty box stays empty and the day stays part-closed and says so. Treating a blank as a count of nothing would invent a shortfall the size of the account, which is the single worst thing a reconciliation screen can do.

THE ACCENT IS CLOSE THE DAY. "Book the missing 5,000" is deliberately NOT the accent: booking a difference writes a real cash-shortage entry and puts a loss on the profit and loss, and the honest first answer to a shortfall is usually not that button — it is finding the entry nobody made. The rail says so before you press anything.

THE RAIL DURING THE COUNT carries what to do before you close, and the month's counting record — days counted, days that matched, the money short across the month. A shop that counts every day and matches every day is a shop nobody can quietly take from, and two-of-four is a number the owner can move.

WHAT TOMORROW OPENS WITH IS WHAT YOU COUNTED, not what the book calculated. That rule already exists in the code; the screen now says it out loud, where the decision is made.

THE MORNING, UN-GATED →

THE BOOK IS ON SCREEN BEFORE IT IS OPENED. Carried figures, each marked with where it came from and whether it was counted or merely calculated, the whole strip in muted ink with "carried, unconfirmed" under the total. One banner, one sentence, two buttons. Confirm is the accent; everything else on the screen steps down, including Add, because on an unopened day confirming the opening is the one thing to do next.

THE ENTRY LINE STILL WORKS. A sale at seven in the morning is not going to wait for somebody to confirm three balances, and the old screen made it wait. It logs against the carried figures and settles when you confirm them.

THE EMPTY LEDGER NAMES THE NEXT ACTION and says what arrives by itself — money taken through Invoices, money paid on a supplier bill — because a shopkeeper who does not know that will double-enter it.

THE OTHER TWO BANNERS ARE STACKED BELOW TO COMPARE THE WORDING. Only one is ever on screen.

THE BROKEN CHAIN is crimson and is the one thing this screen must not let past quietly: a wrong opening figure reconciles PERFECTLY against itself, so the day-end variance can never catch it. It names both remedies and does not pick one for you.

THE FIRST DAY OF THE BOOK is worded differently on purpose. There is nothing to carry and somebody is being taught what a cash book is: everything the book ever says afterwards is measured from those three figures, so it is worth counting twice.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the desk reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 44px hit targets, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS NOT THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are working through the day and closing it. On a phone you are in the yard: somebody has just handed you money, or you want to know what is in the drawer without walking to the office. So the order is what is in each account, then the two things that need a decision, then the movements — and the accent is Log money, docked in the thumb zone, with money on hand beside it so the figure and the act are read together.

THE STRIP IS 2×2 and drops "Money on hand", because the dock carries it permanently at the bottom of every scroll. Nothing else on the phone is ever more than one figure from the truth.

WHAT NEEDS YOUR EYE IS ONE TAPPABLE LINE, not three. You are not auditing in a yard; you are being told there are three to come back to, with the worst one named.

THE MOVEMENT CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON — the card is the tap target, the pattern Creditors and Follow-ups already ship. A transfer row is greyed so it does not read as trading. Money never truncates; the description does.

THE COUNT IS ITS OWN SCREEN, one card per account, 48px count boxes, and the dock says how far through you are and what is wrong before you press Close the day.
